newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil bankers blame brokers in bond fraud.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bankers blame brokers in bond fraud.

text.p: Heads of large Brazilian banks blamed the use of brokers as middlemen for losses incurred by states and cities in a multi-million-dollar municipal bond fraud scheme, newspapers reported on Tuesday.

The Estado de Sao Paulo daily said Lazaro de Mello Brandao, president of giant private bank Bradesco, told senators leading a probe into the alleged racket that his bank would have paid more for the bonds than the intermediaries.
"The ones who lost money are the issuers of the debt," Brandao was quoted as saying.

Brandao testified on Monday to a Parliamentary Committee of Inquiry (CPI) which has been investigating allegations that brokers and officials skimmed up to $400 million off the top of suspect bond issues by some states and cities.

Senators leading the investigation allege the states and cities sold debt at below-market prices to friendly brokerages who in turn passed the securities on at considerable profit to others involved in the scheme.

Officials from Bradesco, federal mortgage bank Caixa Economica, Lloyds TSB Group Plc-owned Banco Multiplic SA, and Parana state bank Banestado were summoned by the CPI to explain why they bought some of the debt and at what price.
In January, the central bank closed down about a dozen brokerages, many of them fly-by-night operations, suspected of involvement in the scheme.
In a statement distributed to reporters before his testimony, Brandao noted that Bradesco "for philosophical reasons" did not take part in the launch of municipal bonds.
"It acquires them in the market, at reasonable prices, and has nothing to do with the way they came into our hands," the statement said.
Market players had previously said they feared the CPI could get out of control if it summoned senior bankers. But in the event, traders said they had other things to worry about.
The probe has targeted Sao Paulo mayor Celso Pitta, who denies any wrongdoing, and also Pitta's mentor and predecessor, presidential hopeful Paulo Maluf.
Maluf has rejected claims he was involved in any way and has condemned the "pornographic profits" made by some brokers.
The CPI has also focused on the Central Bank's role in supervising bond issues, with senators baying for the blood of the bank's public debt department head, Jairo da Cruz Ferreira.
Ferreira has taken a three-month leave of absence from the bank. Officials denied there was any link.
